candidates.attacker_control: The `do` query parameter of a request to the WikiServlet mapping (default `/wiki/*`, e.g. GET /wiki/Main?do=<payload>). No authentication is required to reach the servlet; WikiServlet.doGet handles GET/POST anonymously. The value is taken verbatim (`req.getParameter("do")`) and only a null check is applied.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked whether any validation exists elsewhere: no other component inspects `do` (only ShortURLConstructor.getParameter("do") matched in Java), CommandResolver resolves commands from the `page` parameter/path, and CommandResolver.resolvePage applies MarkupParser.cleanLink to non-existent pages (but this only affects page names, not the forward target). Default configuration uses DefaultURLConstructor, whose getForwardPage returns pathInfo (DefaultURLConstructor.java:278-281) and does not use `do`; ShortViewURLConstructor hardcodes "Wiki.jsp" (ShortViewURLConstructor.java:104-107), so only the ShortURLConstructor mode is affected. The servlet prefixes "/" and appends ".jsp", the container normalizes traversal, and escaping the webapp root is unlikely; target JSPs may also enforce their own <wiki:Permission> checks, which this finding does not bypass. No JSP files are present in the snapshot, so concrete reachable targets (e.g. admin/install pages) could not be enumerated.
candidates.impact: Authorization/forced-browsing bypass: an unauthenticated user can make the server forward to arbitrary JSP resources under the web application through the /wiki/ entry point, reaching pages that are intended to be protected by URL-pattern container security constraints or by request-dispatch filters. Depending on which JSPs exist, this can disclose information or expose functionality (e.g. administrative/management views) that direct access would deny. It is a server-side path-traversal/forward-target weakness; no data-flow beyond the forward is proven.
candidates.prerequisites: Non-default configuration `jspwiki.urlConstructor=ShortURLConstructor` (documented in jspwiki.properties; the default is DefaultURLConstructor) and the default WikiServlet mapping `/wiki/*` from web.xml. The forward target must resolve to an existing `*.jsp` resource inside the web application; the most severe effect (reaching a JSP protected by container-managed authentication or by URI-pattern filters) requires such container constraints/filters to be configured, as the shipped web.xml documents but leaves commented out. Path segments that would escape the webapp root are likely normalized/rejected by the container, so the issue is bounded to in-context resources.
candidates.root_cause: ShortURLConstructor.getForwardPage() takes the raw HTTP parameter `do` and returns it concatenated with ".jsp" without any validation or allow-list (ShortURLConstructor.java:221-227). WikiServlet.doGet() then embeds that value directly into a RequestDispatcher path (WikiServlet.java:96-100), so the attacker controls the resource being forwarded to. `../` segments are resolved by the servlet container, and because filters/constraints are enforced on the original request URI (/wiki/*) and the mapping declares no dispatcher types, the forwarded target is reached without re-applying those protections.
candidates.title: Unvalidated `do` request parameter used as RequestDispatcher forward target (ShortURLConstructor → WikiServlet), enabling traversal/forced dispatch to arbitrary JSPs inside the webapp
candidates.trace: GET /wiki/AnyPage?do=<attacker-value> → WikiServlet (mapped /wiki/*, web.xml:158-161) → doGet reads pathInfo for the page name → m_engine.getURLConstructor().getForwardPage(req) → ShortURLConstructor returns `req.getParameter("do") + ".jsp"` (no validation) → WikiServlet builds `req.getRequestDispatcher("/" + jspPage + "?page=" + encodeName(pageName) + "&" + queryString)` → dispatcher.forward(). With `do` containing `../` sequences (e.g. `do=../admin/SomePage`), the container normalizes to another in-context JSP; because the web.xml filter-mappings (WikiJSPFilter /wiki/* and *.jsp) declare no <dispatcher>FORWARD</dispatcher>, the forwarded JSP is executed without the filter chain that guards direct accesses, and container security constraints (which are evaluated for the original request URI /wiki/…, not the forwarded path) are likewise not re-evaluated for the target.
candidates.unverified: The container's exact normalization behavior for `..` in a RequestDispatcher path and whether any sensitive JSP is reachable could not be executed or confirmed (code/tests were not run; JSP templates are absent from the snapshot). The exact set of protections bypassed (filter vs. container constraint) depends on deployment configuration. I did not confirm a mapping to a specific CVE/known advisory from the snapshot alone, and I could not verify the finding at runtime.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22/CWE-610: externally controlled path used as server-side forward target (path traversal / forced browsing / protection bypass)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 1001 model-visible files (jspwiki-main/java, jspwiki-util, jspwiki-markdown, it-tests, jspwiki-war resources/config/scripts, wiki page bundles); binary files refused/skipped, no symlinks or sensitive-path exclusions were reported, and no JSP or test source files are present in the snapshot. P1 relation index: 1001/1001 files indexed (complete, no hash mismatches), 5439 symbols / 15321 calls / 10593 edges; index labels are navigation hints only and were verified against source text. Reviewed security-relevant flows across servlets and filters, URL constructors, command/page resolution, authentication/authorization, ACLs and permissions, sessions, page/attachment providers, parsers/tags, and utilities; the strongest traceable issue was selected. Coverage is not exhaustive (large files such as JSPWikiMarkupParser and WikiEngine were sampled rather than read end-to-end).
limitations: No JSP pages/templates are included in the snapshot, so template-level sinks and the exact set of dispatch targets reachable via the `do` parameter could not be confirmed.
No test sources are included, so regression/security tests that might document intended behavior for `do`, `skin`, or attachment names were unavailable.
The P1 index provides syntactic call/containment hints only; it does not prove data flow, reachability, or exploitability, and no code was executed or scanned at runtime.

Container behavior (Tomcat/Jetty normalization of '..' in RequestDispatcher paths and re-evaluation of security constraints on FORWARD dispatch) was reasoned about from the code/spec but not verified in this run.
Large security-relevant Java classes (JSPWikiMarkupParser, WikiEngine, Workflow/GroupManager) were reviewed only in relevant sections, not line-by-line.

rejected_leads.lead: PageNameTag prints Attachment.getFileName() and beautifyTitle(page name) without HTML escaping (PageNameTag.java:44-52); AttachmentManager.validateFileName (AttachmentManager.java:637-679) does not strip '<' or '>' from uploaded file names, so a stored XSS via a crafted attachment name appeared plausible.
rejected_leads.reason: The Java sink and the weak filename filtering are visible, but no JSP/template is present in the snapshot to confirm that wiki:PageName is rendered for attachments or non-existing pages (page names are otherwise passed through MarkupParser.cleanLink, which removes <, > and quotes). Reachability is unverified, so it was not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: Serializer.deserializeFromBase64 uses a raw ObjectInputStream.readObject() on Base64 data read from user profiles (Serializer.java:60-71, called from XMLUserDatabase.java:685 and JDBCUserDatabase.java:744).
rejected_leads.reason: The serialized bytes are produced by the application itself (serializeToBase64 writes the profile attribute map) and stored in the user/group database; no path was found where an attacker supplies raw serialized bytes. Exploitability would require direct attacker write access to the DB, so it is a code smell rather than a demonstrated remote vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: HttpUtil.getRemoteAddress trusts the client-supplied X-Forwarded-For header (HttpUtil.java:53-56), which is used for the anonymous login principal (AnonymousLoginModule.java:83), spam/IP-ban checks and the IfPlugin's IP tests.
rejected_leads.reason: Trusting X-Forwarded-For is an intentional reverse-proxy accommodation and the security impact depends on deployment (proxy presence) and on sites having IP-based ACL/policy entries; no evidence of an injected defect or concrete in-snapshot authorization decision that relies solely on this value.

rejected_leads.lead: AttachmentServlet's nextpage/redirect parameter validation (validateNextPage, AttachmentServlet.java:434-449) only rejects values containing '://', so protocol-relative URLs (//evil.example) pass and would be sent via sendRedirect (lines 304, 418, 426).
rejected_leads.reason: Impact is a low-severity open redirect requiring interaction with the attachment servlet, likely long-standing upstream behavior, and no sensitive operation is exposed by the redirect itself.

rejected_leads.lead: CookieAuthenticationLoginModule builds a file path from the raw JSPWikiUID cookie value (new File(cookieDir, uid), lines 213/116) with no uid validation, so a crafted cookie could traverse the work/ logincookies directory and use a readable file's content as the login name.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires non-default jspwiki.cookieAuthentication=true, an attacker-readable/known file whose contents equal a victim user name (or attacker-chosen name), and the file must exist under/next to the cookie dir; the practical exploitation path could not be established from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: Attachment uploads allow HTML/SVG and other active content by default (no forbidden extension list in jspwiki.properties; isTypeAllowed returns true when allowed patterns are empty, AttachmentServlet.java:157-176) and attachments are served with 'Content-Disposition: inline' and a container-derived MIME type (lines 260-270).
rejected_leads.reason: This is a default-configuration/hardening concern rather than a code defect introduced here; serving user-controlled active content inline is a known design trade-off.

summary: Reviewed the JSPWiki 2.11.0.M3-SNAPSHOT source snapshot (1001 visible files; Java main sources plus resources/scripts/config; no test sources and no JSP templates in the snapshot). Broad inspection covered servlets/filters (WikiServlet, WikiJSPFilter, WikiServletFilter, AttachmentServlet, WikiAjaxDispatcherServlet, RPCServlet), URL constructors, command resolution, authentication/authorization managers, ACL/permission parsing, wiki-session state, page providers/attachment providers, parsers/renderers, plugins/tags, and security utilities. One candidate met the evidence bar: attacker-controlled `do` parameter flowing into a RequestDispatcher target in short-URL mode. Several other suspicious areas (unescaped tag output, Java deserialization helper, X-Forwarded-For trust, attachment redirect validation) were examined and rejected or left as unconfirmed leads; details below.
